title: Text objects
summary: Act on a word, a quoted string, a bracket's contents or an HTML tag, wherever the cursor is inside it.

steps.title: inner and a
body: After an operator you can name a **text object** instead of a motion. It does not depend on where in the thing the cursor is.
| `iw` / `aw` | inner word / a word **plus** the space after it |
| `i"` / `a"` | inside the quotes / including the quotes |
| `i(` or `ib` / `a(` | inside the parentheses / including them |
| `it` / `at` | inside an HTML/XML tag pair / including the tags |
`ci"` is the classic: put the cursor anywhere in `"old value"`, type `ci"`, type the new value. On the same line vim even finds the first quoted string to the right if you are not inside one yet.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: The cursor is on the `l` of `"hello world"`. Which keys delete only `hello world`, leaving the empty quotes `""`?
steps.explain: `i"` is the inside of the quotes; `a"` would take the quotes too.

steps.prompt: The line is `print(sum(a, b))` with the cursor on the `a`. You type `di(`. What is the line now?
steps.explain: `i(` selects inside the **innermost** parentheses around the cursor: `a, b`.

steps.prompt: The line is `bold text` with the cursor on the `o`. You type `cit`, then `strong`, then `Esc`. What is the line now?
steps.explain: `it` is everything between the opening and closing tag.

steps.prompt: Match the command to what it changes in `f("a b", [1, 2])`.
pairs: `da(` (cursor on the comma after the quote)
the whole `(...)` with its contents is removed

steps.prompt: Which text does the object include?
Replace the arguments of the call the cursor is inside with `x, y`.
steps.explain: `ci(` empties the parentheses and puts you in insert mode.

steps.title: Find a text object
prompt: Write `(int Start, int End)? Inner(string line, int col, char open)` returning the inclusive column range that `i<open>` selects, for `open` one of `(`, `[`, `{` or `\"`:

- **brackets**: find the nearest unmatched `open` at or before `col` (skip pairs already closed to its right... in other words walk left counting depth), then its matching close to the right. The inner range is from just after the opener to just before the closer. If there is no enclosing pair, return `null`.

- **quotes** (`\"`): take the quote characters on the line in order and pair them up 1-2, 3-4, ...; use the pair that contains `col` (on either quote or between). If `col` is in none, use the first pair that starts after `col`. If none, `null`.
- If the inside is empty (`()`), return `(open + 1, open)`, i.e. `End < Start`.
starter: (int Start, int End)? Inner(string line, int col, char open)
solution: (int Start, int End)? Inner(string line, int col, char open)
for (int i = 0; i < line.Length; i++) if (line[i] == '"') quotes.Add(i);
if (col >= quotes[i] && col <= quotes[i + 1]) return (quotes[i] + 1, quotes[i + 1] - 1);
for (int i = start + 1; i < line.Length; i++)
hints: For brackets, walk left from `col` keeping a depth: a closer (not the cursor's own char) adds one, an opener at depth 0 is yours.
Then walk right from the opener to its partner.
For quotes, collect positions and pair them up two at a time.
template: Dojo.Eq("outer parens from outside the inner pair", ((int, int)?)(6, 14), Inner("print(sum(a, b))", 7, '('));
Dojo.Eq("on the opening paren", ((int, int)?)(10, 13), Inner("print(sum(a, b))", 9, '('));
Dojo.Eq("quotes around the cursor", ((int, int)?)(5, 15), Inner("msg=\"hello world\";", 7, '"'));
Dojo.Eq("first quoted string to the right", ((int, int)?)(5, 15), Inner("msg=\"hello world\";", 0, '"'));
Dojo.Eq("not inside any", ((int, int)?)null, Inner("a (b) c", 6, '('));
